##Part A — Creating Data Frames
```{r}

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)


students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
print(students)


typeof(students$name)
# and class(students$name)
class(students$name)


courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)
print(courses)
```
Question #1: You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline. Both approaches produce the same kind of object. In your own words, explain why data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length, and what error you would expect if they didn’t.   

(A data frame is a strict rectangular table where every column must represent an equal number of rows to maintain grid alignment. If columns had differing lengths, R would fail to pair the observations and return an error stating that the arguments imply a differing number of rows.)

Question #2: A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.” Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?   

(This description works because lists can group independent items of varying data types together into a single container. Consequently, each column vector can maintain its own specific data type, while all columns are bound together by sharing the exact same length.)

##Part B — Subsetting Data Frames
```{r}

students$age
students[["age"]]
students["age"]  

students[2, ]

students[3, "name"]

students[students$passed == TRUE, ]

students[students$passed == TRUE & students$age > 19, ]
```
Question #3: students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects. Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.

(students$age extracts a raw numeric vector, whereas students["age"] extracts a subsetted single-column data frame container. This mirrors lists, where single brackets preserve the container structure and double brackets unpack the raw contents directly.)

Question #4: In the multiple-conditions filter, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19) before that combined result is used to filter rows. What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

(The & operator evaluates both conditions element-wise across each row, requiring both criteria to be true simultaneously. If you used | (OR), rows would be returned if either condition were satisfied, widening the filter to include students who passed even if young, or older students even if they failed.)

##Part C — Data Frame Properties
```{r}

str(students)

dim(students)
nrow(students)
ncol(students)

names(students)

summary(students)
```
Question #5: Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name). Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.   

(R calculates descriptive statistics (mean, median, range) for numeric columns, tallies counts for logical columns, and displays class length for character columns. A mean calculation is invalid for names because character strings represent nominal categories rather than measurable quantities.)

Question #6: str() and summary() both describe a data frame, but they show different information. Based on what you observed, when would str() be more useful to you than summary(), and vice versa?

(str() is more useful when you need to inspect the internal technical data types and structural layout of every column. summary() is more useful when you want a rapid statistical overview and data distribution of the values inside each column.)

##Part D — Data Frame Operations
```{r}

students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
print(students)

students$passed <- NULL
print(students)

students[order(students$age), ]

students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```
Question #7: After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from earlier (students$passed == TRUE)? Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.

(You would get an error because the passed column no longer exists in the data frame object. Keeping track of structure is essential because dropping or modifying columns breaks downstream code that relies on those specific variable names.)

Question #8: order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions. Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).   

(The order() function first computes and returns an integer vector of sorted row positions. The bracket notation then applies this position sequence to rearrange all rows across every column simultaneously.)
##Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
print(grades)

grades$remarks <- c("Passed", "Passed", "Passed", "Passed", "Failed")
  
grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```
Question #9: Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?” Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.   

(You could first create a score difference column to measure the drop between midterm and final exams. Next, you would sort the data frame by consistently low midterm scores and then by the score drop column to see which pattern more reliably correlates with failing grades.)

Conclusion
A data frame is R's core two-dimensional structure for handling heterogeneous tabular data, combining equal-length vectors into rows and columns. It functions essentially as a list where individual columns can hold different data types while sharing a uniform length. This design makes data frames indispensable for real-world data science tasks that require organizing mixed text, numeric, and logical variables.
